summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.field_subfield: Photonics / Topological photonics (optics and wave physics)
summary.executive_summary: Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where light confinement along the third dimension is achieved in a non-topological way and suffers from out-of-plane losses, restricting light flow to planar geometries. This paper introduces a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework that combines a complete photonic bandgap with vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Unlike 2D systems with a single pair of valleys characterized by scalar valley Chern numbers, the 3D model involves triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a diamond-like lattice built from perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by using two spheres of different diameters within each face-centered-cubic cell. This gapping produces a complete photonic bandgap and six valleys grouped into three pairs by time-reversal symmetry. Using the k·p method, they derive an effective Hamiltonian near each valley and show that the Berry curvature has nonzero components only in the plane perpendicular to the valley momentum, verifying vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Experimentally, they use a vectorial chiral source array to selectively excite valley states with valley-locked chirality and observe directional outcoupling at 13.8 GHz, confirming valley-momentum locking. They also demonstrate canalized chiral surface states on all surfaces of a shaped sample and reveal a right-hand-thumb rule relating the valley Chern vectors to the circulating propagation direction of the surface states. The findings highlight applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like crystals.

Executive Summary

This paper introduces a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework that combines a complete photonic bandgap with vectorial valley-contrasting physics. This gapping produces a complete photonic bandgap and six valleys grouped into three pairs by time-reversal symmetry. Using the k·p method, they derive an effective Hamiltonian near each valley and show that the Berry curvature has nonzero components only in the plane perpendicular to the valley momentum, verifying vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Experimentally, they use a vectorial chiral source array to selectively excite valley states with valley-locked chirality and observe directional outcoupling at 13.8 GHz, confirming valley-momentum locking. They also demonstrate canalized chiral surface states on all surfaces of a shaped sample and reveal a right-hand-thumb rule relating the valley Chern vectors to the circulating propagation direction of the surface states. The findings highlight applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, and suggest extension to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like crystals.

Research Context
Valley photonics supplements conventional degrees of freedom to control light. 2D valley photonic crystals host a single pair of valleys with scalar invariants. Valley-contrasting physics underlies vortex and edge states. 2D valley systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. Full 3D confinement requires a complete photonic bandgap, which is challenging.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether 3D topological valley photonics can be realized. The hypothesis is that 3D valley systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys with vectorial invariants. The hypothesis is that these valleys are characterized by valley Chern vectors. The hypothesis is that vectorial valley-contrasting physics governs the system. The hypothesis is that canalized chiral surface states obey a right-hand-thumb rule.

Methodological Details
The study is both theoretical and experimental. The lattice constant is 20 mm. The lattice vectors are defined as a1, a2, and a3. The crystal is a diamond-like lattice with PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres of diameters D1 and D2. Nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods of diameter 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods of diameter 1.2 mm. The rods suppress high-order modes for a clean bandstructure. Inversion symmetry is preserved when the sphere diameters are equal. Inversion symmetry is broken when the diameters differ. The broken symmetry gaps out nodal lines to form a complete bandgap. The six valleys are grouped pairwise by time-reversal symmetry.

Procedures And Architectures
The effective Hamiltonian is derived via the k·p method. The Hamiltonian includes group velocity, Pauli matrices, and a mass term. The mass term is induced by breaking inversion symmetry. The vectorial chiral source array uses four sources. The source positions are set at specific coordinates. The relative phase delays are set for Wy− and Wy+. The valley states outcouple to free-space radiation. The valley momentum is judged from the outcoupling direction. The surface states satisfy the eigenvalue equation and boundary condition. The boundary condition uses a metallic plate with tunable parameters. The boundary condition is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm. The surface states have a linear dispersion traversing the bandgap.

Key Results
The band structure shows nodal chains when the diameters are equal. The diameters are D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm for the gapped phase. The six valleys are located at specific momenta. The eigenstates display opposite chirality at Wz±. The Berry curvature verifies vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The valley Chern vector is (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The outcoupling direction is −32.9° for the clockwise winding. The outcoupling direction is 0° without phase winding. The measured outcoupling is at 13.8 GHz. The radiated beams are single-directional in 3D space. The surface transmission is high within the complete photonic bandgap. The bulk transmission is substantially lower.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature of the 3D valley states is revealed. The valley Chern vectors and propagation direction obey the right-hand-thumb rule. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction. The canalization is an intrinsic property of the surface states. The canalization offers opportunities for imaging and lensing. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation determined by the bulk Hamiltonian.
